tagline: From a former dirt road to lakes shaped by lava and ice
intro: Century Drive climbs steadily from Bend into the Deschutes National Forest, then the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway runs past Mount Bachelor and south along the Cascades. Oregon DOT gives the drive 66 miles and three to five hours. The Federal Highway Administration describes this National Scenic Byway through its lava flows, alpine lakes and meadows. The geological variety is visible from the road: west of Bend, a lava flow that changed the Deschutes River’s course comes into view.

Oregon DOT traces Century Drive’s name to a 100-mile dirt road of horse-and-buggy days. A primitive road from Bend reached Elk Lake in 1920, helping make the lake a summer recreation destination. Growing visitor numbers brought more ranger work, and the Forest Service built Elk Lake Guard Station in 1929 to support that presence.

From Bend, travel west past Mount Bachelor to Todd Lake, then Sparks Lake and Devils Lake. Continue south past Elk Lake toward Lava Lake and Little Lava Lake, where the Deschutes begins. The young river runs through a meadow beside the byway on the way toward Cultus Lake and Crane Prairie Reservoir. Beyond Crane Prairie, the road continues south to Davis Lake and ends at Oregon Route 58 near Crescent and Odell lakes.
notice: West of Bend, a lava flow that altered the Deschutes River’s course is visible from the road.

moments.title: Sparks Lake
moments.text: Sparks Lake loses water through openings along its southwest shore rather than a visible outlet stream. Lava flows from the Three Sisters and Mount Bachelor systems formed its closed basin. Snowmelt from South Sister and Broken Top feeds it. Sediment and vegetation have partly filled what was once a larger lake. Mount Bachelor, the Three Sisters and Broken Top are visible from the lake, putting the water beside the volcanic peaks that frame it. The Forest Service maintains a boat launch here, with a parking area and a trail beside the lake.
moments.notice: Water flows into crevices and outcrops along the southwest shore.

moments.title: Devils Lake
moments.text: At Devils Lake, clear water and a shallow white pumice bottom create an optical illusion: boats can seem suspended above the lakebed. The lake covers 23 acres at an elevation of 5,446 feet. The surrounding volcanic country also became a training ground for astronauts preparing for the Apollo missions in the mid-1960s. Oregon DOT records that Jim Irwin left a rock from a volcanic dome near Devils Lake on the lunar surface during Apollo 15 in 1971.
moments.notice: Clear water lies over a shallow white pumice bottom.

moments.title: Lava Lake
moments.text: Solidified lava separates Lava Lake from Little Lava Lake and is visible along both shorelines. Flows from Mount Bachelor changed the local drainage patterns, forming these neighboring lakes. The two lakes sit in the Deschutes National Forest; Lava Lake’s elevation is 4,740 feet, and Little Lava Lake’s is 4,744 feet. Lava Lake covers 368 acres and averages 20 feet deep. To the north, Broken Top and South Sister rise into view. At nearby Little Lava Lake, the Deschutes starts as a small creek flowing south before its later turn north toward the Columbia.
moments.notice: Solidified lava is visible along the shores of Lava Lake and Little Lava Lake.
